content:
The algebra survives; the interpretation is the problem
A scenario assigning every act the same utility cancels out of their comparison under the stipulated expected-utility model. The failure is identifying the absence of an objectively compelling morality with the absence of valued outcomes. A person can prefer survival without a universal proof of that preference; the author’s eventual rejection of the original wager is justified.

quote: None of these things could have led me astray
content:
The counterfactual cure is untested
Looking backward and identifying loose reasoning can explain how an error became possible. It cannot establish that sufficient rigor would have prevented every serious mistake: rigorous reasoning can start from false data, omitted hypotheses or a misspecified model. The stronger claim needs more than an autobiography whose ending selects the lesson.

quote: No, you don’t use the best concepts
content:
Acting under uncertainty is unavoidable
Demanding a better understanding before a consequential step can be wise. But waiting, researching and declining to act are also choices with uncertain consequences. Nature’s indifference to excuses cannot establish that a decision made with the best available model was irrational; the relevant comparison is among feasible options at the time.

content:
A useful interface can precede an explanation
A black box can be unacceptable when safety depends on its unknown internals. It can also be a legitimate scientific or engineering object when its relevant behavior is measured and its domain of reliability is explicit. A blanket demand to open every box confuses incomplete mechanistic understanding with an absence of usable evidence.
